transcript: If you arrive on the scene: Check the scene for safety. Check the infant for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder or flick the bottom of the heel and shout. No Response: Call 911 immediately. If the infant is lying on their stomach, turn them over onto their back. They should be lying on a hard flat surface. Check for Breathing and signs of life: Watch their chest for any normal movement. Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. No Breathing or signs of life. Begin CPR: a. Position 2 or 3 fingers on the center of the infant's breastbone, just below the nipple line. b. Compress the chest 1½ inches in depth 30 times. c. After giving compressions, give breathes. Tilt the infant's head back, slightly, using one hand on the forehead and lifting up on the infant's chin with two fingers of your other hand. Cover both the infant's nose and mouth with your mouth and give 2 small slow breaths, watching for the infants chest to rise. d. Continue with 30 compressions/2 breathes, 30 compressions/2 breaths, etc. Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

title: PEDIATRIC CPR Explained Simply
description:
Pass School & NREMT Exams, Go Here: https://www.prepareforems.com

Get my EKG/12-Lead EKG Masterclass: https://www.ekgforems.com

Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) according to the American Heart Association (AHA) involves specific steps tailored to infants and children up to puberty. The process begins with ensuring the scene is safe for both the rescuer and the patient. Once safety is confirmed, check the child’s responsiveness by gently tapping and shouting. For infants, you should tap the bottom of the foot. If there is no response, activate the emergency response system. If you are alone with a child or infant and there is no response, perform CPR for 2 minutes before leaving to call emergency services. If another person is present, have them call emergency services immediately.

Next, open the airway using the head-tilt-chin-lift technique. Be careful with the amount of tilt, especially in infants. Check for breathing and a pulse for no more than 10 seconds. For infants, check the brachial pulse, and for children, check the carotid or femoral pulse. 

For chest compressions in infants (under 1 year), use two fingers in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line, pressing to a depth of at least 1.5 inches (4 cm) at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute. For children (1 year to puberty), use one or two hands (depending on the size of the child) on the lower half of the breastbone, pressing to a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm), but not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm), at the same rate of 100-120 compressions per minute.

After compressions, provide rescue breaths. For both infants and children, give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions (or 15:2 if two rescuers are present). Each breath should last about 1 second and make the chest rise visibly. Use an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) as soon as it is available. For infants and children under 8 years, use pediatric pads if available. If not, use adult pads, placing them so they do not touch each other. Follow the AED prompts and resume CPR immediately after each shock, continuing until the child shows signs of life or emergency medical personnel take over.

Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths (or 15:2 if two rescuers are present) until the child shows signs of life, an AED is ready to use, or professional help arrives. These steps ensure that CPR provided to pediatric patients follows the AHA's guidelines for optimal outcomes.

title: How to give CPR to a child
description:
If you see an infant or child collapse, CPR can save their life. Rescue breaths are especially important when performing CPR on a child in cardiac arrest. To give CPR to a child, call 911, push hard and fast in the center of the chest. After 30 compressions, give two rescue Repeat until help arrives.

Be ready to save a life. Find a CPR class at https://www.heart.org/nation.
transcript: Products are shown for demonstration  purposes only. The American Heart Association does not endorse or recommend  any specific manufacturer or products. If you see an infant or child suddenly collapse  it is important to act fast. Helping to save a life is easier than you might think. Child CPR  is similar to adult CPR but it is especially important to give breaths to a child who  needs CPR. A child in cardiac arrest who is unresponsive and not breathing normally  will not survive without CPR. Your actions can help increase their chances of surviving  if you're alone. CPR on infants and children should always include breaths done in cycles of 30  compressions followed by two breaths. First check to make sure the scene is safe. If you're near  anything that can hurt you or the child move to a safe place. Next tap the child's shoulders and  shout are you OK. If the child is unresponsive shout for help. Point to someone and ask them to  call 911 and get an AED or call 911 yourself and put your phone on speaker mode so the operator  can help you. Now check for breathing scan the chest for 5 to 10 seconds looking for it to rise  and fall. If the child is not breathing normally immediately start CPR. With the child flat on  their back kneel beside them and lean directly over their chest. Place the heel of one hand or  two hands one on top of the other in the center of the chest. Then push hard and fast in the  center of the chest giving 30 compressions. It is important to keep a steady beat of 100 to 120  compressions per minute, which is about the same tempo as the song “Baby Shark” or the rate  of the music that you are hearing right now. Push down about 2 inches, about the height of  a credit card, letting the chest return to its normal position between compressions. Now after 30  compressions you'll give two breaths one after the other that makes the chest rise. Put one hand on  the forehead and the fingers of your other hand under the chin. Tilt the head back slightly and  lift the chin to open the airway. Pinch the nose, take a normal breath and cover the mouth with  your mouth, giving one breath for 1 second while watching for chest rise. Give another breath.  Don't stop compressions for more than 10 seconds to give breaths. Continue giving cycles of 30  compressions and two breaths until help arrives. [Music]

Transcript:
You Arrive on the Scene

Check the scene for safety. Check the infant for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder or flick the bottom of the heel and shout.

No Response

Call 911 immediately.  

If the infant is on his or her stomach, turn the infant over onto his or her back.  The infant should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch the chest for any normal movement.  Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR

a. Position two or three fingers on the center of the infant’s breastbone, just below the nipple line.

b. Compress the chest 1½ inches in depth 30 times.

c. After giving compressions, give breaths. Tilt the infant's head back, slightly, using  one hand on the forehead and lifting up on the infant's chin with two fingers of your other hand. Cover both the infant’s nose and mouth with your mouth and give two small, slow breaths, watching for the infant’s chest to rise.

d. Continue with 30 compressions / two breathes, 30 compressions / two breathes, etc. 

Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

transcript: [CHIMING] CPR is a life-saving action that can get oxygen and blood to the brain in an emergency. Getting trained in CPR is the best way to be prepared, but knowing the basics can help save a life. If a baby doesn't seem to be breathing, shout and tap the bottom of the feet and see if there's any response. Lay the baby face up on a flat, firm surface. Kneel or stand to one side. You may be taught to check for breathing by seeing if the chest is moving, but don't spend more than 10 seconds doing this. Next, shout for help. Have someone call 911 and get an AED, Automated External Defibrillator, if possible, while you start CPR. If you're alone and have a phone, call 911 and then begin CPR. Leave the phone on speaker. If you don't have a phone, do five rounds of CPR, then look for a way to call 911. Start with chest compressions. Place both thumbs side by side in the center of the baby's chest, just below the nipple line, with your other fingers wrapping around, towards the back, like this. You can also do compressions by placing the heel of one hand in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line. Push down fast and hard, about 1.5 inches deep. Let the chest come back up completely after each compression. Do this 30 times. Try to do about two compressions a second. After every 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. To open the airway, tilt the head back and lift the chin. Put your mouth over the baby's nose and mouth and blow in for about one second. Use just enough air for the chest to rise. After the chest rises and falls, give the second breath. If the chest doesn't rise, reposition the head and chin and try again. Keep doing compressions and rescue breaths until the baby stirs or wakes up or help comes and takes over. Use an AED as soon as one is available. Don't touch patient. Analyzing. transcript: Hi, my name's Nick and welcome to this short lecture on CPR for pediatrics, which is a follow-on from the adult CPR lecture. Thankfully, it's a lot rarer for children to go into cardiac arrest than it is for adults. The guidelines for healthcare professionals who have a duty to respond in a pediatric emergency are slightly different to the adult guidelines with a bigger emphasis on ventilations. This reflects the fact that the more likely cause of a pediatric cardiac arrest will be asphyxia as opposed to a primary cardiac event in an adult. For the purpose of the guidelines, an infant is referred to as an under 1-year-old. The child is from 1 to 18, and an adult is over 18. Since we don't always have this information immediately to hand, if it looks like a baby, assume it's a baby. If it looks like a child, then it's a child. And if it looks like an adult, then it's an adult. The initial approach is the same as for an adult. Check for danger. Check for responsiveness, usually by pinching or flicking. Never shake an infant. Then shouting for help. The way we open the airway will vary a bit depending on the size of the child. In an infant, the airway should be opened with a head in the neutral position and a chin lift. As the child increases in age, a small degree of head tilt chin lift will be required, progressing further up to a full head tilt chin lift in adulthood. With the airway open, look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for no longer than 10 seconds. Infrequent noisy gasps can occur in cardiac arrest and are not a sign of normal breathing. Assuming someone has responded to your shout for help, get them to call the pediatric cardiac arrest team on 2222, stating clearly that it's a pediatric cardiac arrest and the ward location twice. Start by clearing the airway if necessary and attempting five rescue breaths. With an infant, use your mouth over their mouth and nose, and in a child, pinch their nose and use mouth-to-mouth. Remember that your lungs are a lot bigger than theirs, so give just enough volume to make their chest rise over a duration of 1 to 1 and 1/2 seconds. If the chest hasn't risen after five attempts, then move on. The airway may be blocked. After these five attempts, check for a pulse and other signs of life for no longer than 10 seconds. In an infant, use the brachial or femoral pulse, and in a child, use the carotid or femoral pulse. Assuming there's no pulse and no signs of life, or a pulse of less than 60 in a moribund apneic infant or child, then we can presume cardiac arrest. We perform 15 compressions to rate of 100 to 120 a minute. When compressing an infant or a child's chest, we aim to compress at least 1/3 of the depth of the chest. In an infant, we do it by using two fingers or two thumbs. In a child, use one or two hands to compress the chest depending on the size of you and the size of the child. Once the 15 compressions have been performed, then attempt another two breaths, and then continue CPR to ratio of 15 to 2. If you're ever on your own, perform 1 minute of CPR before going for help. Remember that in these circumstances, doing something is always better than doing nothing. I hope you never have to use these guidelines for real.

transcript: If you ever find your baby is not responding to you, you will give them the best chance of survival if you know what to do. If you have found your baby unresponsive and not breathing normally, you'll need to perform baby CPR. Call for help. Ask a helper to call 999 or 112 for emergency help. Use a mobile speakerphone if you're on your own, so you can start CPR as soon as possible. If you're on your own and you don't have a speakerphone, you need to do CPR for a minute before you can call for help. Place them on a firm surface and open their airway. With one hand on the forehead, gently tilt their head back. With your finger tip, gently lift the chin to open the airway. Pick out any visible obstructions from the mouth and nose. Step one is 'puff'. Take a breath, put your lips around your baby's mouth and nose make a seal. Blow gently and steadily for up to one second. The chest should rise. Remove your mouth and watch the chest fall. That's one rescue breath or 'puff'. Do this five times. Step two is 'pump', or chest compressions. Put two fingers in the centre of your baby's chest and push down a third of the depth of the chest. Release the pressure, allowing the chest to come back up before pressing back down again. Repeat this 30 times at a rate of 100-120 pumps per minute. This is quite quick. After 30 chest pumps, open the airway and give a further two puffs. Continue to alternate between thirty chest pumps and two puffs. If you're on your own and don't have a speakerphone, stop after one minute and call 999 or 112 for emergency help. If a mobile phone is not available and you have to move to get to a telephone, take the baby with you. Keep repeating 30 pumps then two puffs until help arrives or they become responsive. So remember: if your baby's unresponsive and not breathing, call for help. Ask a helper to call 999 or 112 for emergency help. If you're on your own use the speakerphone and start CPR soon as possible. If you don't have a speakerphone, do CPR for a minute before calling for emergency help. Give five initial puffs, covering both the nose and mouth, then 30 chest pumps with two fingers to the centre of the chest. Continue CPR with 30 pumps and two puffs until help arrives. And that's how you do baby CPR. Thanks for watching. Help support St John Ambulance. Donate today.

title: How to Perform Emergency CPR on an Infant - Royal Life Saving Training Video
description:
Disclaimer - This video is for training purposes only. If it is an emergency please call Triple Zero (000). 

To find out more about enrolling in a Resuscitation course with Royal Life Saving visit:   https://www.royallifesaving.com.au/training/resuscitation

A family member is the first on the scene in most emergency situations. In fact many children are alive today because their parents knew how to perform CPR and responded quickly. For this reason alone, Royal Life Saving encourages everyone to learn CPR.

Having the skills to respond in an emergency situation can mean the difference between life and death.

Resuscitation or Cardio Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) involves stimulating the heart and breathing air into the lungs to preserve or restore life. Resuscitation involves establishing or maintaining an airway, breathing and circulation.

Royal Life Saving has a number of CPR related resources and courses available including a CPR chart that can be used near your backyard swimming pool and CPR courses that are run in a variety of locations across all States and Territories.

transcript: If after performing a primary survey, you find a child who is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call for help. Ask someone to phone 999 or 112, and ask them to bring an AED if one is available, while you begin CPR immediately. If you're by yourself and do not have a speakerphone, start CPR with five initial rescue breaths, then 30 chest compressions and 2 rescue breaths for one minute before calling for help. To give rescue breaths, open the airway by tilting the head back with one hand on the forehead and two fingers under the chin. Pick out any obstructions from their mouth to clear the airway only if you can clearly see something. Keeping the head in this position, pinch the soft part of the nose. Allow the mouth to fall open. Take a deep breath and seal your mouth around theirs. Blow steadily into their mouth, giving a rescue breath in about one second. The chest will rise. Remove your mouth from theirs and watch their chest fall. Give them five initial rescue breaths at about one breath per second, like this. To do chest compressions, kneel down by child, beside their chest. Place only one hand on the centre of the chest. Lean over the child with your arms straight and press down vertically one-third of its depth. Release the pressure. Allow the chest to come back up without removing your hand from the chest. Repeat this to give 30 chest compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute. This is quite fast and to help you, you can sing Nellie the Elephant, which can help you to keep up with the pace. After thirty chest compressions, open the airway and give them a further two rescue breaths. Continue to alternate between thirty chest compressions and two rescue breaths until help arrives. If you're on your own and don't have a speakerphone, stop after one minute and call 999 or 112 for emergency help If a mobile phone is not available and you have to move to get a telephone, take the child with you if you are able. Do not leave the child to look for an AED - the emergency services will bring one with them. If there is someone there who can help, if they brought an AED, ask them to turn it on and follow instructions while you continue CPR. If they can help you perform CPR, you can swap over every one to two minutes with minimal interruptions to chest compressions. Continue CPR until emergency help arrives and takes over, the child starts to show signs of becoming responsive, they start breathing normally or opening their eyes, or you become too exhausted to continue. If they do start breathing normally again, put them in the recovery position. So remember: if you come across a child that's unresponsive and not breathing normally, call for help. Tell a helper to call 999 or 112 straightaway and ask them to bring an AED. Give five initial rescue breaths Then thirty chest compressions followed by two rescue breaths. Continue giving 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths until help arrives, or the child starts to breathe. And that's how we perform CPR on a child. If this video has been helpful to you, help support St John Ambulance by going to sja.org.uk/donate

https://www.propals.io - PALS Certification Training Videos - Get $20 off your certification or recertification with the discount code youtubepals2017

If a baby does not respond and is not breathing normally, call 911. Check for a brachial pulse for no more than 10 seconds. If there is no pulse, begin CPR on the infant. CPR should be performed with two fingers in the center of the chest, on the sternum, between the nipples for 30 compressions followed by two breaths. Repeat this process until EMS arrives, an AED becomes available, or advanced life support arrives.

transcript: As a new parent, learning CPR is very important. Thousands of babies are saved every year because someone knew CPR and started it right away. Knowing CPR can help prevent brain damage in your child if they stop breathing. CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation. CPR helps keep blood and oxygen flowing to the heart and brain when the heart stops. In this video you will learn the basics of infant CPR. Infant CPR is only for babies less than a year old. CPR for children and adults is slightly different. Anyone who cares for an infant should, and can, learn CPR. (Speaker #1) If you find your baby unresponsive or not breathing… 1. Tap the baby’s foot and shout to see if they respond. Never shake a baby. 2. If the baby does not respond, yell for help. 3. If someone comes, tell them to call 911. 4. Check for breathing. 5. If the baby is not breathing, they need CPR right away. 6. Carefully move the baby to a firm, flat surface, above ground. 7. Place two fingers in the middle of the baby’s chest, just below the nipple line. 8. Give 30 compressions by pressing straight down about 1 ½ inches. 9. Push hard and fast, at least 100 compressions per minute, and let the chest rise all the way back up after each push. 10. Next, give two breaths by putting your mouth over the baby’s mouth and nose. 11. Gently give enough breath to make the baby’s chest rise. 12. Keep alternating two breaths and 30 compressions until the baby responds or trained help arrives. If the baby is still unresponsive after two minutes of CPR and you have no help to call 911, carry the baby with you to the phone, and make the call yourself. You can continue giving compressions and breaths with the baby in a football hold. Every five days in the United States, at least one child dies from choking. When an infant is choking, quick action can be lifesaving. Continue watching to learn what to do when a child is choking. If a baby is choking but is able to cough and breathe, allow them to do so. It allows their own reflexes to clear the airway. If you know a baby is choking and they are having trouble breathing or they stop breathing, begin a sequence of five back slaps and five chest thrusts. This is what it looks like: 1. Hold the baby face down on your forearm with its head lower than its body. Make sure the baby’s head and neck are supported. 2. Give five firm slaps on the baby’s back with the heel of your hand. Deliver the slap between the baby’s shoulder blades. 3. If the object does not come out, turn the baby over onto their back. 4. Support the head and neck with your arm, and keep the baby’s head below their body. 5. Now give five chest thrusts. Use two fingers and press down in the middle of the baby’s chest just below the nipple line, like you did in CPR. 6. Repeat five back blows and five chest thrusts until a. The object is coughed up b. The baby begins to breathe, or c. The baby becomes unconscious 7. If the baby becomes unconscious, follow the steps of infant CPR that you’ve already learned 8. Each time you give breaths, look to see if the object has come out. 9. If you see an object in the mouth, take it out. Any baby that receives CPR or choking treatment should be seen by a doctor to make sure they’re all right. Thank you for watching this video. Please practice with a nurse and on a mannequin until you feel comfortable doing it on your own.

title: How to perform Child CPR with an AED
description:
If you see an infant or child collapse, CPR can save their life. Rescue breaths are especially important when performing CPR on a child in cardiac arrest. To give CPR to a child, call 911, push hard and fast in the center of the chest. After 30 compressions, give two rescue Repeat until help arrives.

If an AED is available, follow the prompts to provide a shock to try to restore a normal heart rhythm.

Be ready to save a life. Find a CPR class at https://www.heart.org/nation.
transcript: Products are shown for demonstration  purposes only. The American Heart Association does not endorse or recommend  any specific manufacturer or products. If you see an infant or child suddenly collapse  it is important to act fast. Helping to save a life is easier than you might think. Child CPR  is similar to adult CPR but it is especially important to give breaths to a child who  needs CPR. A child in cardiac arrest who is unresponsive and not breathing normally  will not survive without CPR. Your actions can help increase their chances of surviving  if you're alone. CPR on infants and children should always include breaths done in cycles of 30  compressions followed by two breaths. First check to make sure the scene is safe. If you're near  anything that can hurt you or the child move to a safe place. Next tap the child's shoulders and  shout are you OK. If the child is unresponsive shout for help. Point to someone and ask them to  call 911 and get an AED or call 911 yourself and put your phone on speaker mode so the operator  can help you. Now check for breathing scan the chest for 5 to 10 seconds looking for it to rise  and fall. If the child is not breathing normally immediately start CPR. With the child flat on  their back kneel beside them and lean directly over their chest. Place the heel of one hand or  two hands one on top of the other in the center of the chest. Then push hard and fast in the  center of the chest giving 30 compressions. It is important to keep a steady beat of 100 to 120  compressions per minute, which is about the same tempo as the song “Baby Shark” or the rate  of the music that you are hearing right now. Push down about 2 inches, about the height of  a credit card, letting the chest return to its normal position between compressions. Now after 30  compressions you'll give two breaths one after the other that makes the chest rise. Put one hand on  the forehead and the fingers of your other hand under the chin. Tilt the head back slightly and  lift the chin to open the airway. Pinch the nose, take a normal breath and cover the mouth with  your mouth, giving one breath for 1 second while watching for chest rise. Give another breath.  Don't stop compressions for more than 10 seconds to give breaths. Continue giving cycles of 30  compressions and two breaths until help arrives. [Music] Hopefully you never have to perform  CPR on a child. When possible use an AED - automated external defibrillator -  in your life-saving efforts. When the AED arrives use it immediately. Once the AED has  arrived place the child face-up on a firm, flat surface and follow the prompts of the AED.  Try not to interrupt compressions for more than 10 seconds. [Music] Turn the AED on and follow the prompts, which  will tell you everything you need to do. You must remove clothes and anything else that covers  the chest as AED pads must be placed directly on bare skin. If necessary wipe the chest dry.  Place pads on the chest. Use the smaller child pads if they are available. If child pads are not  available use the larger adult pads. Peel away the backing from the pads. Follow the pictures on  the pads attach them to the child's bare chest. Ensure there is nothing between the pad and the  child's bare skin. Plug the pads connected into the AED if necessary. Follow the prompts and let  the AED analyze the heart's rhythm. Make sure no one is touching the child and loudly state CLEAR.  The AED will analyze the heart rhythm. If the AED says that a shock is not needed, resume CPR. If  the AED advises a shock is needed make sure no one is touching the child and loudly state CLEAR.  Push the shock button to deliver the shock and immediately resume CPR with 30 chest compressions  and two breaths. Most AEDs will prompt you to analyze the rhythm again after about 2 minutes  of CPR. Keep doing cycles of 30 compression in two breaths and continue following the AED prompts  until the child begins to respond or help arrives. Hopefully you will never have to use CPR on a  child but know that CPR combined with using an AED provides the best chance of saving a life.  If possible use an AED every time you provide CPR. Again, if you see a child suddenly  collapse don't be afraid to start CPR. Your actions can help save a life.  To learn more visit heart.org/nation.

To find out more about enrolling in a Resuscitation course with Royal Life Saving visit:   https://www.royallifesaving.com.au/training/resuscitation

A family member is the first on the scene in most emergency situations. In fact many children are alive today because their parents knew how to perform CPR and responded quickly. For this reason alone, Royal Life Saving encourages everyone to learn CPR.

Having the skills to respond in an emergency situation can mean the difference between life and death.

Resuscitation or Cardio Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) involves stimulating the heart and breathing air into the lungs to preserve or restore life. Resuscitation involves establishing or maintaining an airway, breathing and circulation.

Royal Life Saving has a number of CPR related resources and courses available including a CPR chart that can be used near your backyard swimming pool and CPR courses that are run in a variety of locations across all States and Territories.

title: How to do CPR on an Adult (Ages 12 and Older)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-adults 
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Adult CPR (Ages 12 and Older).

Transcript:
You Arrive on the Scene

Check the scene for safety. Check the victim for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder and shout.

No Response

Call 911 immediately.

If the adult is on his or her stomach, turn the person over onto his or her back. The person should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch the chest for any normal movement. Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR

a. Position the heel of one hand on the center of the adult’s chest.  Place your other hand on top.

b. With your elbows locked and arms straight, lean over the adult and compress the chest 2 inches in depth 30 times.

c. After 30 compressions, give breaths by tilting the head back, lifting the chin and pinching the nose. Give two slow and gentle breaths. The chest should rise with each breath.

d. Continue with 30 compressions / two breaths, 30 compressions / two breaths, etc. 

Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

For more information visit: http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-adults

transcript: (How to do infant CPR) What we're going to teach today,  is how to do infant CPR or  Cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Once you've assessed that the infant is not breathing and is not alert in  any way, you need to call for  help and that's very important. Remove any clothing that the child may have on. You'll want to put your fingers right in the inner aspect of the arm and feel for a pulse. You should  only feel for a pulse for five to ten seconds. Make sure that the infant is on a flat surface as much as possible and a hard surface. You'll want to take your two fingers, your index finger and your middle finger, and place it right in the middle of the breastbone or the sternum underneath the two nipple lines. And you'll want to begin compressions, pushing down on  the chest and allowing the  chest to come up, down on the chest, up, down on the chest, up,  and you want to do this for 30 beats so, one, two, three, four, five. Don't worry, you're not going to push too hard, I promise. So you push hard enough, and you do that for thirty beats. After you've done the thirty chest compressions, you'll then move quickly to the head of the baby, and you will want to give rescue breaths. The first thing you want to do is, tilt the head back, and lift the chin up, so that you open up the airway. You'll then pinch the nose with one hand, and you will deliver a rescue breath over one second and you should have sufficient air blowing into the baby to see both of the  chest walls rise. Like this: (demonstrates breathing) And you'll want to do that twice. So you do 30 chest compressions, and you give two rescue breaths. Immediately when you finish the two rescue breaths, you go back to doing chest compressions. If you are the only person there, then you start chest compressions and rescue breaths for two minutes and then you need to leave the side of the infant and call 911 for help. transcript: Your toddler can go from eating normally to choking in seconds. Here is your refresher. First, take a CPR and first aid course. Seriously. Watching a real here on Instagram is not the same thing. But if it's been a while, here is your refresher. If your child is coughing, forcefully, crying, talking, or making good sounds, their airway is still moving air. Don't immediately start pounding on them or sticking your fingers in their mouth. Encourage them to cough and just watch closely. Many kids will gag or cough the food back up on their own. But if they suddenly can't cough effectively, can't speak or cry, can't breathe, or are turning blue now you have a severe obstruction. Act right now. If multiple people are around, have somebody call 9 1 1 immediately. But realistically, with a complete airway obstruction, you cannot wait for emergency services to arrive. You need to act right away while help is on the way, as it will likely be too late and your child may die before they can get to you. Please do not blindly stick your finger into their mouth. If you can clearly see the food, of course try to remove it, but blindly sweeping around can push the object further back, making things much worse for a toddler or child over the age of one. Current guidance is five firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then five abdominal thrusts. For the abdominal thrust, put your fist just Above the belly button and below the breastbone. Then pull sharply inwards and upwards. Repeat 5 and 5 until the object comes out and the child becomes. Or the child becomes unresponsive. And yes, these need to be forceful. You are trying to create enough pressure to expel something out that is blocking their airway. A bruise or a broken bone is a much smaller problem than not being able to breathe. If they become unresponsive, start CPR, beginning with chest compressions, and follow your emergency training while 9 1 1 is on the way. And don't forget, prevention matters just as much. Toddlers should sit while eating. No running around the house with their food in their mouths. Be especially careful with small, round or firm foods like grapes, hot dogs, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and similar choking hazards. Cut grapes and hot dogs lengthwise into appropriate small pieces. Please save this, send it to grandparents, babysitters, and anyone who watches your kids, and then go take the actual CPR course.
